name: task-workspaces
description: Manage isolated development tasks using Git worktrees and coding agents.

commands.title: Fix One Thing in This Stage…
Send Findings Back to an Earlier Stage…

taskWorkspaces.worktreeParentDir.markdownDescription: Directory in which new worktrees are created. If empty, worktrees are created as siblings of the repository (`<repoParent>/<repoName>-<slug>`). Supports absolute paths.

taskWorkspaces.branchPrefixes.description: Allowed branch type prefixes offered when creating a task workspace.

taskWorkspaces.defaultBaseBranch.description: Default base branch for new worktrees. If empty, the repository's current HEAD branch is used.

oneOf.description: Path relative to the repository root, copied to the same relative path in the new worktree.

from.description: Source path. Relative to the repository root, or absolute.

to.description: Destination, relative to the new worktree. Required when 'from' is absolute.

taskWorkspaces.copyIntoWorktree.markdownDescription:
Files and directories copied into each new worktree after it is created. A fresh worktree contains only tracked files, so untracked local config (for example `.claude/settings.local.json`) has to be brought across.

Entries are either a repository-relative path — copied to the same relative path — or `{ "from": "...", "to": "..." }` where `to` is relative to the worktree. Destinations that escape the worktree are refused. A missing source is logged and skipped, never fatal.

Example: `[".claude/settings.local.json", { "from": "C:/shared/.env.local", "to": ".env.local" }]`

taskWorkspaces.harnessConfigPath.markdownDescription:
Location of this project's harness config: the **routes** work travels through and the **review rules** a change obliges. Relative to the repository root, or absolute to share one config across repositories. Defaults to `.taskworkspaces/harness.json`, falling back to `.taskworkspaces/review-rules.json`.

Always read from the repository root, never from a task worktree, so a branch cannot relax its own review requirements. Create one with **Task Workspaces: Create Harness Config**.

taskWorkspaces.reviewRulesPath.markdownDescription: **Deprecated** — use `#taskWorkspaces.harnessConfigPath#`, which covers routes as well as rules. Still honoured when set and the newer setting is empty.

taskWorkspaces.claudeCommand.description: Command used to launch the Claude Code CLI.

enumDescriptions: Open the task's worktree in a new window and launch Claude Code's own chat UI (requires the anthropic.claude-code extension).
Run Claude headless and show a built-in chat panel inside this window.
Run Claude in an integrated terminal.
taskWorkspaces.agentMode.description: How to start Claude for a task. 'native' uses the official Claude Code extension's chat in the worktree window; 'chat' uses the built-in panel; 'terminal' uses an integrated terminal.

taskWorkspaces.trackNativeActivity.markdownDescription: Show best-effort live activity (working / awaiting input) for **native**-mode tasks by watching Claude Code's session transcripts. This reads an undocumented on-disk layout and may lag or miss; disable to only track built-in chat sessions.

taskWorkspaces.compactPromptThreshold.markdownDescription: When a chat session's context grows beyond this many tokens, the panel prompts you to compact it. Set to `0` to disable the prompt.

taskWorkspaces.autoCompactThreshold.markdownDescription: When a chat session's context grows beyond this many tokens, `#taskWorkspaces.contextStrategy#` is applied automatically at the end of the current turn (no prompt). Set to `0` to disable. Recommended to set this higher than `#taskWorkspaces.compactPromptThreshold#` so you are warned first and only acted on if you keep going — e.g. `160000`.

taskWorkspaces.pauseOnPermissionDenial.markdownDescription:
Stop a route when the CLI's permission layer refuses a tool call, so the permission can be granted before the stage runs again.

A headless stage session has nobody to approve anything, so any call not covered by `permissions.allow` is refused. The agent then rewords the command, retries, and eventually works around it — and a stage that could not run a command it judged necessary has not done its job, so carrying on buries that behind whatever it did instead. The subtask is left pending, so granting the rule and advancing runs it again.

Turn this off to be told about refusals without stopping the route.

taskWorkspaces.interactivePermissions.markdownDescription:
Hold a refused tool call open until you approve or deny it, instead of letting it fail.

A headless stage session has nobody to approve anything, so any call not covered by `permissions.allow` is refused; the agent then rewords it several times and works around it, and the stage has to be re-run once a rule is added. With this on, the extension installs a `PreToolUse` hook that pauses the CLI and puts the call in the task tree. Approving lets the agent carry on **mid-turn** — no re-run, and no rule needed just to unblock it.

The first attempt at a capability is still refused by the CLI: that refusal is what tells the extension a human is needed, and it is an attempt the agent made anyway. Its retry is what gets held.

taskWorkspaces.gatedTools.markdownDescription:
Tools the permission gate is installed for. Empty uses the default set: `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Write`, `Edit`, `NotebookEdit`.

Only these tools reach the hook, so anything left out costs nothing. Adding `Read` or `Grep` is not recommended: they are the calls a stage makes most, and the CLI already permits them.

taskWorkspaces.permissionWaitMinutes.markdownDescription:
How long a held tool call waits for your decision before the CLI gives up on it.

On expiry the call is refused as it would have been anyway, and the route continues or stops per `#taskWorkspaces.pauseOnPermissionDenial#`. Raise it if you want a route to sit waiting while you are away.

taskWorkspaces.holdEveryToolCall.markdownDescription:
Hold **every** gated tool call for approval, not only capabilities the CLI has already refused.

Off by default, and rarely what you want: it stops the agent on calls the CLI would have permitted, including ordinary file writes inside the worktree. Turn it on only when you want to watch exactly what a route does.

taskWorkspaces.projectDocsPath.markdownDescription:
Where this project keeps its own documentation — business rules, data flows, structure. Named to every route stage, which is told to **read** it before exploring the code and to **update** it when the work establishes durable knowledge of that kind.

This is the harness's only lasting memory. Each subtask runs in a fresh session, so a stage otherwise re-derives whatever the previous one worked out and discards it when the session ends; a document in the repository is the one place a finding survives.

Stages are told not to record progress notes, change summaries, or anything the code already states plainly. Set to empty to disable — a project with no documentation convention should not be told to invent one mid-task.

taskWorkspaces.mcpConfigPath.markdownDescription:
MCP server config loaded explicitly into every agent session, via the CLI's `--mcp-config`. Relative to the repository root, or absolute. Set to empty to disable.

Each task worktree is a directory the CLI has never seen, so a project-scoped `.mcp.json` inside it is unapproved — `enabledMcpjsonServers` stays empty and none of its servers start. Non-interactive sessions skip the trust *dialog*, which is not the same as granting trust, and a route's headless sessions have nobody to answer a prompt. Passing the config explicitly is what actually loads the servers.

Read from the **repository root**, never a task worktree, so a branch cannot grant itself new tool access. Existing user-scope MCP servers are unaffected (`--strict-mcp-config` is not used).

taskWorkspaces.stageTimeoutMinutes.markdownDescription: Hard stop for a single route subtask, so a hung CLI cannot stall a route forever. A stage that hits this is recorded as **failed**, so prefer a generous value: planning or investigation stages on a large repository legitimately take tens of minutes, and per-process overhead on the machine (on-access virus scanning of every process launch, most often) multiplies that. Whatever the stage produced before the cap is kept in the log.

taskWorkspaces.askTimeoutMinutes.markdownDescription:
How long a stage may block on an `ask_user` question before the CLI gives up on the call.

Deliberately much longer than **Stage Timeout Minutes**, which bounds a *hung* CLI — a stage waiting on a person is not hung. The harness exists so one engineer can supervise several tasks at once, so a question waiting while you work on another task is the designed case, not an edge case.

Left at the CLI's own default the call times out after a few minutes, the agent proceeds on its own assumptions, and the stage that asked precisely because it did not know is recorded as done. A question still unanswered when the session ends now **fails** the subtask rather than passing silently.

taskWorkspaces.linkSiblings.markdownDescription:
Sibling repositories to link **beside** the worktrees, so relative paths committed into a project keep resolving.

A project that references a sibling as `..\..\QubeData\QubeData.csproj` resolves it correctly from a checkout next to that sibling, and incorrectly from a worktree parked one level deeper. A `Directory.Build.props` can probe for the sibling and fix *project* references, but a `.sln` cannot — solution files take no MSBuild properties, so the path written in them is the path that must exist.

Each entry is either a target path (`"C:\\Dev\\qubedata"` — the link takes the folder's own name) or `{ "name": "QubeUtils", "target": "C:\\Dev\\qube-utils-c" }` when the reference spells it differently from the clone. Relative targets resolve against the repository root.

Created as junctions on Windows, which need no elevation. Idempotent, and **a path that is not already a link is never touched** — if a real folder is in the way, it is reported and left alone.

taskWorkspaces.stageSubagentConcurrency.markdownDescription:
How many subagents a single route stage may run at once (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`, set only for stage sessions).

The harness owns concurrency at the **task** level — the point of it is supervising several tasks at once. Left at the CLI's own default a single stage may run twenty subagents, which does not finish that stage twenty times sooner; it starves every other task of the machine and the rate limit they share, and the loss appears as "everything was slow today" rather than as anything attributable.

Chat sessions you drive by hand are unaffected.

taskWorkspaces.stageSubagentDepth.markdownDescription:
How deep subagent spawning may nest inside a route stage (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH`, set only for stage sessions).

One level by default: a stage delegating to subagents is ordinary, a subagent delegating further is a tree whose cost and duration nothing in the harness predicted. Nesting multiplies against the concurrency cap rather than adding to it.

enumDescriptions: Run /compact: summarise the conversation in place and continue in the same session.
Ask the agent for a written handoff, then continue in a fresh session briefed from it.
taskWorkspaces.contextStrategy.markdownDescription: What to do when a session crosses `#taskWorkspaces.autoCompactThreshold#`. `compact` summarises in place, so context regrows from the summary. `checkpoint` writes a handoff (decisions, remaining work, next step), starts a fresh session from it, and keeps the carried-forward brief size-capped — slower to trigger, but context does not accumulate across the whole task.

taskWorkspaces.model.markdownDescription:
Default model for agent sessions, passed to the CLI's `--model`. These are family aliases — each resolves to the *latest* model in that family, so they stay current as new versions ship. Empty uses the CLI default. You can also set a specific model id (e.g. `claude-opus-5`) by editing this value directly, or switch per-session from the chat panel header.

A route stage can override this with its own `"model"` in `harness.json`, which is usually the better lever: once per-process overhead is dealt with, model time dominates a route, and stages differ enormously in what they need. Reading files to decide where a change belongs is not the same work as writing a migration that will run against a live database.

enumDescriptions: Prompt according to your normal Claude settings.
Auto-accept file edits; prompt for other actions.
Planning only — no changes are made.
Skip all permission checks (use with care).
taskWorkspaces.permissionMode.markdownDescription: Permission mode for chat-panel sessions. Because the headless panel cannot yet show interactive per-action prompts, `acceptEdits` or `plan` are recommended.

taskWorkspaces.gateInterpreter.markdownDescription:
Program used to run the permission gate hook script. Must be able to run a CommonJS file passed as its first argument.

Set an absolute path if `node` is not on the PATH the CLI inherits. If it cannot run, the gate quietly does nothing and refusals behave as they did before — check the Task Workspaces log for `Permission gate`.

taskWorkspaces.stageMcpServers.markdownDescription:
Servers from the project MCP config that sessions this extension starts will load — route stages and task chats alike. Empty means all of them.

Every subtask runs a fresh CLI, and the CLI starts every server in the config before doing any work. A stage pays that cost per subtask, twice over: the startup wait, and the tool definitions each server injects into the context of a session that will never use them. A build stage does not need a set of database servers to compile something.

The cost is worth naming even when everything is healthy — but it is severe when a server *cannot* connect, because the CLI waits out a timeout per server. One project measured nine servers, eight of them unreachable, at over three minutes before the first token of work.

Names are matched case-insensitively. A name matching no server is treated as a mistake and the project config is used unchanged, so a typo cannot silently strip every tool.

Applies to task chat as well as stages. It was stages only, on the reasoning that a chat is exploratory and might want any tool — but the wait is identical, and a person sitting in front of it notices three minutes far more than a subtask does. Clear this list to get all of them back.

Narrowing the set also passes `--strict-mcp-config`, without which the worktree's own approved config starts every server anyway and the reduction achieves nothing. That *also* drops your user-scope servers, which is more likely to be missed in a chat than in a stage.

Only ever *removes* servers, so it cannot widen what a task branch can reach — which is why it is safe alongside reading the config from the repository root.

taskWorkspaces.advanceAfterAnswering.markdownDescription:
Advance the route automatically once you have answered all of a stage's questions, or approved a stage.

Answering and approving are both deliberate acts whose only purpose is to unblock the route, so the confirmation afterwards only created a window in which the task sat idle.

Turn this off to be asked first. Either way, progress shows in the status bar and **Stop Agent** interrupts it.

taskWorkspaces.interactiveQuestions.markdownDescription:
Let a stage ask you a question without ending its session.

The extension runs a small MCP server exposing an `ask_user` tool. When a stage lacks information it calls the tool, pauses, and your question panel opens; answering hands the answer straight back and the agent carries on **mid-turn** with everything it had already worked out.

Without this, a stage that needs information replies `NEEDS-INFO` and ends. Answering then appends to the brief and the subtask **runs again from the beginning** — so the information costs a stage rather than a pause. That path remains the fallback whenever the tool is unavailable.

Requires `node` (see `#taskWorkspaces.gateInterpreter#`). The extension grants itself one permission rule, `mcp__taskworkspaces__ask_user`, in a settings file it owns; without it the CLI refuses the call and the agent reports that it cannot ask.
